analysis.one_liner: Taxes 70% of large bonuses paid by federal bailout recipients and caps their deferred pay.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan backing from 14 senators and placed on the Senate calendar, never received a vote in the 22 months before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that took more than $100 million in federal bailout money, plus Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, would have paid a 35% excise tax on "excessive" bonuses paid to any of their employees or directors, and the bonus recipients would have paid another 35% themselves — a combined 70% tax on bonuses above $50,000, including retention bonuses. Employees who repaid their bonuses to the government would have been spared the tax. The bill also capped at $1 million per year the pay executives at these firms could shelter in deferred-compensation plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who put up hundreds of billions of dollars in bailout funds under the 2008 emergency stabilization program. The 70% excise tax would have clawed back a share of the large bonuses those firms paid out with federal support, and the deferral cap would have stopped executives at rescued firms from sheltering more than $1 million a year from immediate taxation.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a combined 70% excise tax on excessive bonuses — a 35% tax on the company and a 35% tax on the employee — for any bonus above $50,000 (and all retention bonuses) paid by a firm holding more than $100 million in outstanding federal rescue assistance, or by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac.
Applies to any director, officer, or employee of a bailout recipient, not just top executives, and is triggered for firms until their outstanding assistance falls back to $100 million or below.
Exempts employees who repay their bonuses, giving bonus recipients a direct incentive to return the money.
Caps nonqualified deferred compensation at bailout-recipient firms at $1 million per participant per year, closing a channel executives otherwise use to defer income out of current taxation.

analysis.who_pays: Officers, directors, and other employees of bailout recipients who took large bonuses, who would owe an extra 35% tax on top of income tax, and the firms themselves — big banks and insurers in the TARP program and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — which would owe the other 35% and face new withholding and reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and employees at bailed-out firms

drawbacks.text: The tax applies retroactively to bonuses paid after December 31, 2008 — in many cases before the bill was written — so bonus recipients would be taxed at a rate that did not exist when the payments were made, a basic fairness objection to retroactive taxation.
The $50,000 threshold and the definition of 'covered individual' reach any employee of a bailout recipient, including mid-level staff, not only the executives whose pay drew public outrage.

A heavy new tax on bonuses at distressed firms could make it harder to keep the people needed to wind down or repair those companies; the bill itself acknowledges this by carving out equity pay that vests three years or later after the grant.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For taxpayers the upside is real but narrow: it recovers part of the bonus money paid by a specific, defined group of rescued firms, rather than recovering bailout funds generally, and retention of key staff was a genuine concern the bill only partly addresses. The retroactive application is the hardest part to defend, and the $50,000 line sweeps in some employees far from the executive suite. On balance the costs fall on a small, identifiable group that received public money, while the benefits spread across all taxpayers — a trade most people would accept, and one that drew bipartisan sponsorship from 12 Democrats and 2 Republicans.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the middle of the AIG bonus uproar, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar — and then it simply sat there for the rest of the Congress without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Max Baucus, chair of the Finance Committee, introduced the bill on March 19, 2009 with eleven other senators, including the committee's ranking Republican Chuck Grassley and Republicans Olympia Snowe and Susan Collins's colleague list also featuring Democrats such as Schumer, Kerry, and Wyden.
The bill was introduced days after public fury over bonuses paid by rescued insurer AIG, and targeted exactly the firms that had received large federal rescue money.
On March 23, 2009 it was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 37 — a holding position with no vote scheduled.
No committee markup, no floor debate, and no roll call ever followed; the last action in the record is that March 23 placement, and the Congress ended January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bonus recipients at bailed-out firms and the firms themselves came out ahead: they kept large post-rescue bonuses without the 70% excise tax, and taxpayers did not recover any of it through this bill.

for.name: Max Baucus
for.role: U.S. Senator from Montana; Chair, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and submitted introductory remarks on March 19, 2009.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; Ranking Member, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan standing at the top of the Finance Committee.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for a floor vote; it remained on the Senate calendar from March 2009 until the Congress ended.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly cautioned Congress in March 2009 against rushing punitive bonus-tax legislation and pursued executive-pay limits through bailout contracts and Treasury pay rules instead; the White House lent no push toward a Senate vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — 12 of 58 Democrats and 2 of 40 Republicans signed on — and no one ever voted against it, because no vote ever happened; the bill died of inaction, not opposition.

industries.industry: Financial firms rescued with more than $100 million in federal bailout aid (TARP and Federal Reserve programs), plus Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
industries.note: Each firm would owe 35% of every excessive bonus it paid, plus new withholding, notice, and reporting duties, and could not escape the tax except by paying its rescue money back below the $100 million threshold. Firms had paid these bonuses with the help of federal funds, so the industry's interest in keeping them ran against the taxpayers who supplied the rescue.

industries.industry: Executives and high-earning employees of bailout recipients
industries.note: Bonus recipients would owe an added 35% tax on any bonus above $50,000 (and on all retention bonuses), on top of regular income tax, and could defer no more than $1 million a year in nonqualified deferred compensation. The bill's repayment carve-out was the only way to avoid the tax entirely.
